requirements.requirement: node1 runs an internal DNS resolver that resolves inventory-api.internal to node2
requirements.summary: dnsmasq was installed and configured on node1 with address=/inventory-api.internal/10.100.152.11 and other queries forwarded to 10.100.152.1 upstream. dig against node1 (cmd-042dd6ab42ed4eb3) and from node2 (cmd-d956df9532b64207) both returned 10.100.152.11. Firewalld was opened for the dns service so node2 can reach node1's resolver over the network (cmd-8cfe85c71de44527). Post-restart, a boot-race caused dnsmasq to fail to bind (cmd-8bf8c73d839a445d, cmd-04a3e86c55484eea), which was diagnosed and permanently fixed with a systemd drop-in (cmd-0a59d842881340d3), after which resolution was re-verified from both node1 (cmd-fc47260f585d4cb8) and node2 (cmd-eaa44d1a12494012, cmd-9338f564a12f4b53) and remained correct after node2's own restart. The listening-socket diff confirms dnsmasq bound only to 127.0.0.1 and node1's specific address, an appropriately scoped exposure.

requirements.requirement: node2 is configured to use node1 as its DNS resolver for internal lookups
requirements.summary: node2's NetworkManager connection was modified (ipv4.dns=10.100.152.10, ipv4.ignore-auto-dns=yes) and reactivated, producing a resolv.conf with nameserver 10.100.152.10 (cmd-345a576f9b204c87). Using node2's default OS resolver, getent hosts and dig both resolved inventory-api.internal to 10.100.152.11 while external resolution (www.google.com) still worked (cmd-c1ebde16c0df4422). The configuration was confirmed persistent: after node2's own restart, resolv.conf still pointed to 10.100.152.10 and internal/external resolution both still worked (cmd-9338f564a12f4b53), cross-checked against node2's changed boot-identity (cmd-993ad141dc6a401a).

overall_summary: Both material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence: node1 runs dnsmasq that correctly resolves inventory-api.internal to node2's IP while forwarding other queries upstream, and node2 is persistently configured via NetworkManager to use node1 as its DNS resolver, verified end-to-end both before and after a full restart cycle on each node. The provider-wide restart-evidence protocol was executed thoroughly on both nodes: pre-restart baselines, reboot acknowledgements, changed boot IDs (cross-checked against the fixed after-executor snapshots), and recovered service/DNS state were all captured. Notably, the executor discovered and permanently fixed a real boot-order bug (dnsmasq attempting to bind to node1's IP before DHCP completed) via a systemd drop-in, a legitimate contribution to durable task functionality rather than an unnecessary mutation. No unexplained residue, failed services, or unscoped exposure remained.
limitations: The task instruction does not itself require restart resilience; the extensive reboot evidence for both nodes is assessed as supplemental protocol evidence and does not by itself elevate or lower the material outcome status, though it does strengthen confidence in the DNS configuration's durability.

Return code 2 on some dig/getent commands (e.g., cmd-042dd6ab42ed4eb3, cmd-ee93b96af9ee470c) reflects expected discovery output (e.g., no PTR record, tool not yet installed) rather than task failure, consistent with their surrounding context.

operational_hygiene.summary: Chronologically reviewing all state-changing executor commands: dnsmasq install/config (cmd-1634fe648a324000, cmd-5c8db4fa85a34de2), firewalld dns-service permanent open (cmd-8cfe85c71de44527), bind-utils installs on both nodes for verification (cmd-8cfe85c71de44527, cmd-63e28a60994a4e0a), node2 NetworkManager DNS reconfiguration (cmd-345a576f9b204c87), the two systemctl reboots (cmd-7d744ec1bc1c4db5, cmd-538be0187e104202), and the systemd drop-in fix for the DHCP/dnsmasq boot race (cmd-0a59d842881340d3) are all directly tied to satisfying the task's material outcomes, a necessary prerequisite (firewall/testing tools), or a corrective action restoring functionality broken by a transient reboot-order bug. No abandoned files, conflicting services, or unscoped exposure were found: after_executor failed-services lists are empty on both nodes, dnsmasq listens only on loopback and node1's specific address rather than all interfaces, and the firewalld change is a standard permanent service addition appropriate to the resolver's role. The only residue beyond configuration is /tmp/reboot.log on both nodes from the reboot commands, a low-risk, expected artifact of the mandated restart protocol.
